stories.headline: MLB Power Rankings Week 23: Top teams in first September edition
stories.summary: As the season enters the stretch run, our top 10 remains mostly the same while teams on the fringe of the playoffs continue to try and make a push.
stories.body:
Welcome to the stretch run of the 2026 MLB season! As we enter September, some of baseball's top teams are cruising to a playoff berth, while others are making their final pushes for a chance to play in October.

Three powerhouse National League teams are vying for not only MLB's best record, but for the top two seeds in the NL bracket, which would secure them first-round byes. Meanwhile, in the American League, the East winner should determine the No. 1 seed, with an unlikely contender seemingly a lock for the second seed.

Certain divisions, such as the NL West, are basically decided, and the top two wild-card teams in each league have solid leads, leaving multiple teams fighting for a chance to secure the third spot. One of those contenders in the AL was our biggest riser of the week, with the Orioles up five spots to No. 14 and just 1½ games out of the final wild card.

Our expert panel has ranked every team based on a combination of what we've seen so far and what we already knew going into the 162-game marathon that is a full baseball season. We also asked ESPN MLB experts Buster Olney, David Schoenfield and Jesse Rogers to weigh in with an observation for all 30 teams.

Week 22 | Second-half preview | Preseason rankings

1. Milwaukee Brewers

Record: 87-53

Previous ranking: 1

Jacob Misiorowski is just weeks away from wrapping up his first Cy Young award and could be the first qualified pitcher this decade to record an ERA of 1.70 or below. As is, he's the lone pitcher in either league with an ERA under 2.00. Braves star Chris Sale is about the only competition for the award, but unless Misiorowski implodes, he's the clear cut winner. That wasn't necessarily the case at the All-Star break, but it is now after a masterful five months. -- Rogers

2. Los Angeles Dodgers

Record: 82-57

Previous ranking: 2

The Dodgers don't need Shohei Ohtani to pitch to win their third straight World Series. They employ a surplus of quality starters. But Ohtani wants to pitch, and the Dodgers are giving him the chance to return to the mound. The four-time MVP hasn't pitched in a game since July 3 because of knee and biceps injuries. His attempt to return for a one-inning start Sunday against the Tigers was aborted after a shortened 20-pitch bullpen session Friday. With a little over three weeks remaining in the regular season, getting him on track to pitch in games will be difficult considering he plays every day. But the Dodgers aren't abandoning the notion yet. They're going to let him try. -- Castillo

3. Atlanta Braves

Record: 83-57

Previous ranking: 4

Holding onto first place in the NL East and earning a bye should clearly be the goals for the Braves in September. Their strength of schedule might have a say in that, though, as they have the fifth-toughest road ahead. It includes seven games against the second-place Phillies as well as a series against the playoff-bound Cubs and Rays. But it's those showdowns with the Phillies that will be the difference-maker -- and it starts with a four-game wrap-around series this weekend in Philadelphia. Atlanta has been the class of the East all year. They have one more month to prove it once-and-for all. -- Rogers

4. Tampa Bay Rays

Record: 83-56

Previous ranking: 5

When Tampa Bay added Freddy Peralta at the trade deadline, rival executives immediately speculated that Peralta would rebound from his four rough months in New York at the outset of this season with the help of the Rays' staff -- and that seems to be happening. Over his last two outings, Peralta has allowed just one run in 12 innings, while continuing to work a much greater percentage of changeups into his pitch mix. With Peralta, Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and Shane McClanahan, Tampa Bay can ably match up in a short series with any American League rival. -- Olney

5. Chicago Cubs

Record: 78-62

Previous ranking: 3

It's Pete Crow-Armstrong's world -- we're just living in it. A strong month of September will likely secure him his first MVP award to go along with what should be another Gold Glove honor and perhaps even the Platinum Glove. Meanwhile, he's not far from exceeding 10.0 in fWAR right now, which means 11.0 could be in sight. It's rarified air for what's turning into the game's best position player. PCA has one month left of a historic season that could also include a 40/40 campaign. -- Rogers

6. New York Yankees

Record: 80-60

Previous ranking: 6

As Aaron Judge moves closer to returning to the Yankees' lineup -- perhaps during the next homestand -- the overriding question will be: How quickly can he return to form in the 15-to-18 games he could play before the postseason? He'll have about 60 to 70 plate appearances in that time. At 6-foot-7, Judge has a challenge in attempting to quickly restore his swing against a generation of pitchers who will likely attack him with velocity at the top of the zone. Over time, Yankees' staffers say, Judge has learned to do more with less work, a skill that could help him in trying to catch back up. -- Olney

7. Philadelphia Phillies

Record: 79-61

Previous ranking: 7

The Phillies were red hot in August, going an MLB best 21-7. It's put them in a position to chase down Atlanta for the NL East title, but can they carry that play over into September? It took a lot of energy for the Phillies just to get to this place, so it wouldn't be shocking if there was some regression, but then again, they understand the need for a first-round bye and beating out the Braves might just get them one. It's pedal-to-the-metal time for Philadelphia as Bryce Harper's quest for a championship hangs in the balance. -- Rogers

8. Boston Red Sox

Record: 75-65

Previous ranking: 8

Roman Anthony and Trevor Story returned to the Boston lineup over the weekend in New York, and Garrett Crochet continues to make progress in his effort to play some kind of role for Boston in the last days of this season, as well as in the postseason. Coming back from a shoulder issue, Crochet threw off a mound last week -- and presumably, if all goes well, he'll throw to hitters sometime later this month. Remember, he was a dominant reliever for the White Sox before transitioning to a starting role. -- Olney

9. San Diego Padres

Record: 73-67

Previous ranking: 9

The Padres called up 20-year-old catcher Ethan Salas when rosters expanded Tuesday, giving their top prospect his first taste of the big leagues in the middle of a tight playoff race. The left-handed-hitting Salas made his major-league debut Wednesday, going hitless in four at-bats against the Reds. With the appearance, he became the youngest player to catch in a big-league game since Ivan Rodríguez in 1991. One of baseball's most hyped prospects in recent years, Salas batted .296 with 10 home runs and an .822 OPS in 96 games this season between Double-A and Triple-A. -- Castillo

10. Chicago White Sox

Record: 73-66

Previous ranking: 11

With Chicago leading the AL Central, general manager Chris Getz added veteran outfielder Tommy Pham in a deal with the Phillies. Getz was trying to add more outfield depth to the organization, he explained in a text, and added that Pham could help against left-handed pitching. "And on top of it, Pham offers a veteran presence," Getz said, "that can help limit September or postseason vibrations." -- Olney

11. Arizona Diamondbacks

Record: 74-67

Previous ranking: 10

The Diamondbacks are in the middle of a heated race for the final NL wild-card spot, but that hasn't garnered the spotlight in the desert. That instead has been focused on Ketel Marte, who returned to the field Monday two weeks after another unexcused absence left the club scrambling without answers. While Marte, who was activated from the injured list with mild inflammation in his left knee, said teammates welcomed him back into the clubhouse, Diamondbacks fans greeted the three-time All-Star second baseman with loud boos in a 2-1 loss to the Phillies. The Diamondbacks will now look to move on from the strange episode as they battled the Padres for their first postseason berth since their 2023 World Series run. -- Castillo

12. Cleveland Guardians

Record: 70-69

Previous ranking: 12

During the Terry Francona and Steven Vogt managerial years, Cleveland has historically finished strongly -- only the Dodgers have a better September/October winning percentage than Cleveland since the start of 2013 -- and now the Guardians have won nine of their last 12. With the playoff push underway, Chase DeLauter hit .363 in August while Steven Kwan hit .347, and Jose Ramirez is seemingly hitting with more authority. -- Olney

13. Houston Astros

Record: 71-69

Previous ranking: 15

Yordan Alvarez entered September with a legitimate chance to win the first Triple Crown since Miguel Cabrera in 2012. He leads the AL with a .317 batting average and 94 RBIs while tied for first in home runs with Junior Caminero at 37. Alvarez also leads the AL in on-base percentage and slugging percentage. He's been the best hitter in the majors this season and is the heavy favorite to win AL MVP. Alvarez would join Ohtani as the only primary designated hitters to ever win the award. Fueling the Astros to a postseason berth and becoming the second Triple Crown winner since 1967 would easily cinch the honor. -- Castillo

14. Baltimore Orioles

Record: 69-71

Previous ranking: 19

What a difference one game in the standings seems to make with the Baltimore front office. On Aug. 1, the Orioles were just 1½ games behind in the race for the third wild card in the AL, and yet they moved Taylor Ward, Adley Rutschman and Dean Kremer at the deadline. Then, on Aug. 31, with the O's within a half-game of the wild card and a month to play, they decided to add, taking on the last $4 million or so of Luis Robert Jr.'s 2026 contract. In spite of the incongruous decisions, the players are still pushing for a playoff spot. -- Olney

15. Miami Marlins

Record: 71-69

Previous ranking: 13

It's been over a decade since a Marlin led the league in hits -- Dee Gordon was the last to accomplish that feat in 2015. Otto Lopez has a chance to do it after earning 26 hits in 27 games played during August. He has 165 hits heading into the final weeks of the season, giving him an outside chance at 200 -- a rare feat in this day and age of MLB. Either way, Lopez has taken another positive step in his career. -- Rogers

16. Texas Rangers

Record: 69-71

Previous ranking: 14

Nathan Eovaldi threw Tuesday for the first time since going on the IL on Aug. 10 with elbow inflammation. He told reporters he expects to pitch again this season after throwing 50 pitches on flat ground. Getting him built up to a starter's workload, however, will be a challenge at this point in the calendar. Whether it's in the rotation or the bullpen, the Rangers could use the 36-year-old right-hander for their playoff push. -- Castillo

17. Toronto Blue Jays

Record: 69-71

Previous ranking: 18

Despite a shocking regression in the production of Vladimir Guerrero Jr., a crushing early-season injury to Alejandro Kirk and a measured teardown by the Jays' front office at the trade deadline, Toronto is somehow still alive and relevant in the race for the third wild-card spot in the AL. With strong August performances from George Springer, Brett Bateman, Dylan Cease, Shane Bieber and Max Scherzer, the Jays are making one last drive for a playoff spot that would be almost as stunning as Toronto's advancement to Game 7 of the World Series last fall. -- Olney

18. Pittsburgh Pirates

Record: 68-72

Previous ranking: 21

Since making the postseason is out of the question once again for the Pirates, they should concentrate on finishing at least .500 for the first time in a full year since 2018. That's a lot of futility through an ongoing -- some might even say everlasting -- rebuild. This is easily their best team this decade, but despite a positive run differential, the Pirates are still languishing under break-even. Their offense -- a question mark coming in -- has been good. It's their pitching staff, including Paul Skenes, that has underachieved. A big month by either might just get them to that .500 mark. It's something. -- Rogers

19. St. Louis Cardinals

Record: 70-70

Previous ranking: 16

Continued development on the mound should be the Cardinals' goal during the final month. They've gotten answers from around the diamond as Alec Burleson and Jordan Walker had career years while JJ Wetherholt might have taken home Rookie of the Year honors if not for a hand injury slowing him down. But St. Louis needs to figure out its rotation for next season, as there have been mixed results in a group that includes Michael McGreevy, Andre Pallante, Matthew Liberatore and Kyle Leahy. Most of the ups and downs of the season were good experience. A strong finish could set the Cardinals up for a resurgent season in 2027. -- Rogers

20. Minnesota Twins

Record: 67-73

Previous ranking: 20

Minnesota has faded in its effort to win a wild-card berth in the AL, and it still has series ahead against the White Sox, Yankees and Rangers, among others. The Twins made as big of a value bet as possible to get into the postseason, opting to keep pending free agent Ryan Jeffers and ace Joe Ryan at the trade deadline. They also never seriously explored the trade return of Byron Buxton, who has a no-trade clause and would've had to approve any deal. Minnesota's effort to reach the postseason may well turn out to be very costly. -- Olney

21. Washington Nationals

Record: 67-75

Previous ranking: 23

CJ Abrams is poised to join the 30/100 club this month, the first such season of his career. It should help him pass 5.0 fWAR for the first time as well. Any concerns that he's not a big-time player were eliminated this year as he and James Wood combined to make a lethal duo in Washington. A career high in home runs and RBIs to go along with 30-plus steals would cement Abrams as one of the better players in the league and someone to build around. Even in today's game, you don't see those numbers from many shortstops. -- Rogers

22. Seattle Mariners

Record: 66-74

Previous ranking: 17

Cal Raleigh's historic dropoff has rightfully garnered the headlines, but he isn't the only star underachieving in Seattle this season. Julio Rodriguez, another franchise pillar, is batting .245 with a 104 wRC+ while his defense has taken a massive step back. His blunder on a line drive off Roman Anthony's bat Monday night set the stage for a backbreaking walk-off loss. In addition to J-Rod, Josh Naylor has a .692 OPS in his first year of a five-year, $92.5 million contract, Bryan Woo has a 4.36 ERA, George Kirby has a 4.19 ERA and closer Andres Munoz has a 4.35 ERA. Concocting the most disappointing season in franchise history has been a group effort. -- Castillo

23. Detroit Tigers

Record: 64-75

Previous ranking: 22

After the Tarik Skubal trade, the Tigers' brass talked about still trying to compete for a playoff spot. Instead, Detroit will go into its last month trying to stay out of last place in the AL Central. A rival evaluator noted that Skubal seemed to be the Tigers' superpower, capable of beating any team in any situation on any day -- and without Skubal, Detroit has looked like a completely different team. In games Skubal was on the team's active roster this year, the Tigers were 40-33. Without him, they are 24-42, including getting thumped 15-2 on Tuesday. -- Olney

24. Cincinnati Reds

Record: 67-73

Previous ranking: 24

He leads the league in games played and in RBIs -- and he's just a rookie. Sal Stewart lived up to the hype this year and looks to be the next great Reds hitter. A 40-homer, 120-RBI season is not out of the question. Only three rookies have ever hit 40 or more home runs, and even if Stewart falls short, he's a lock to win the Rookie Of the Year award. If the Reds can surround him with some protection in the lineup moving forward, those numbers might be just the beginning of a great career in the Queen City. -- Rogers

25. New York Mets

Record: 63-77

Previous ranking: 25

The Mets need a productive month from Mark Vientos simply to feel like his career can get back on track. They've said positive things about him, but now he needs to back that up after missing almost two months with a fractured hand. Vientos has been on a steady decline since helping the Mets to the NLCS in 2024, dropping from a career-high 27 home runs that season to just 12 this year. Missing time obviously hurt him, but his miniscule batting average (.214) and on-base percentage (.258) tell the story of his season. -- Rogers

26. Kansas City Royals

Record: 62-78

Previous ranking: 26

Kansas City has a legitimate shot at surpassing Detroit -- and perhaps even Minnesota -- before the end of the regular season, as the Royals' 2027 team continues to take shape in a strong finish at the end of the '26 season. Jac Caglianone and Noah Cameron have played great since the All-Star break, and amid the rubble of this season, the front office can continue to project a lineup and rotation for next year. Since Aug. 16, the Royals rank tied for fourth among all teams in runs scored. -- Olney

27. San Francisco Giants

Record: 58-82

Previous ranking: 27

Not much has gone right for the Giants in 2026, but they'll go into 2027 with two dangerous left-handed sluggers in the middle of their lineup. There's the veteran Rafael Devers, the former Red Sox malcontent who leads the club with 32 home runs, 83 RBIs and an .837 OPS. Then there's the rookie Bryce Eldridge, a towering slugger who has found his stroke in his first extended stint in the majors. Just 21 years old, he has 15 home runs and an .806 OPS in 94 games. The Giants have a long list of deficiencies. Left-handed pop isn't one of them. -- Castillo

28. Los Angeles Angels

Record: 53-87

Previous ranking: 28

Two months after firing general manager Perry Minasian, owner Arte Moreno agreed to sell the Angels to Stan Kroenke for a record valuation of $4 billion Tuesday in a deal that will be completed in early 2027. Moreno bought the franchise in 2003. His 24th and final season as owner will end like the previous 11: With the Angels failing to reach the playoffs. It's the longest postseason drought in the majors. Kroenke will attempt to steer the organization back to October. -- Castillo

29. Athletics

Record: 54-86

Previous ranking: 30

With so many regulars on the IL for the remainder of the season, the final month represents an opportunity for players to make a case for a spot on the 2027 team. Shea Langeliers (knee), Nick Kurtz (thumb), Jacob Wilson (shoulder), Brent Rooker (knee) and Tyler Soderstrom (hip) are all out. It's been that kind of year for the A's. The silver lining would be finding a few pieces to help the team in their final season in West Sacramento before making the move to Las Vegas in 2028. -- Castillo

30. Colorado Rockies

Record: 54-86

Previous ranking: 29

TJ Rumfield was stuck in Triple-A when the Yankees traded him to Colorado for reliever Angel Chicilli in January. The low-profile move has paid big dividends for the Rockies. Alongside All-Star catcher Hunter Goodman, Rumfield has been one of the team's two best hitters this season. The 26-year-old first baseman is batting .291 with 14 home runs and an .826 OPS in 136 games this season, while his 3.3 bWAR leads the club. The Rockies are building their foundation for their next contention window, and it figures to include Rumfield. -- Castillo

stories.headline: How Bueckers, Clark, Reese will impact Team USA at World Cup
stories.summary: The future is here for Team USA as Paige Bueckers, Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and others make their debut in a major event.
stories.body:
A picture from 2017 resurfaces occasionally on social media. In it, a younger Caitlin Clark, Paige Bueckers and Aliyah Boston wear USA Basketball gear, huddling somewhere at the U.S. Olympic Training Center in Colorado Springs, Colorado, and flashing thumbs up and peace signs.

They had been in the cold tubs amid preparations for the FIBA Americas U16 Championship, Bueckers recently recalled to ESPN, probably after a dreaded two-a-day session. The photo also features Azzi Fudd -- who like the other three would later become a No. 1 WNBA draft pick -- and former Stanford standout Fran Belibi.

"We were all down bad hurting at such a young age," Bueckers said.

"I don't think any of us probably would have guessed we would have all made it [to this level], and that the WNBA is what it is now with the amount of attention that's on us," Clark told ESPN. "But at the same time, I think we would all say it's pretty cool. It's kind of like a pinch me moment."

Over the next 10 days, Clark, Bueckers and Boston will again share the court representing the United States with a slew of younger WNBA stars in Angel Reese, Kiki Iriafen and Sonia Citron at the FIBA World Cup in Berlin.

The group of transcendent players, with their on-court talent and off-court relevance, catapulted the WNBA into a new era of popularity. Now they are tasked with helping Team USA secure its 12th World Cup gold medal and fifth straight.

"There's always pride when you wear USA," Boston told ESPN. "I think it's kind of a full circle moment for us to be in the big girl jerseys now."

The future -- or as Bueckers quipped in December, the "Young and Turnt" crew -- is here. And they're perhaps even younger, and being thrown into the fire, even more than anticipated.

USA Basketball announced Monday that Team USA stalwarts A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum will not compete in Berlin due to health reasons. Those decisions led to Iriafen and Citron getting called up to join the group.

The U.S. women's team has six players under the age of 25, tied for the most on a USA World Cup or Olympic roster since 1994. With Rhyne Howard, 26, also on the squad, seven of the 12 players have never represented the senior national team in either major international 5-on-5 tournament, tied for the second-most such players on a USA roster since 1994.

But none of that matters when a gold medal is on the line. The standard for USA Basketball, which has lost one game at the World Cup or Olympics since 1994, remains the same -- even as it has become more difficult than ever to win on the international stage, as the United States' one-point win over France at the Paris Olympics' gold medal game illustrated.

"There's no question that the world is improving at a rapid rate," U.S. coach Kara Lawson said Tuesday. "I think it's going to be the most difficult World Cup to win that we've had because of that."

THE ORIGINS OF the "Young and Turnt" generation for USA Basketball might have come from that 2017 U16 team, but the players' arrival onto one of the sport's biggest stages was far from guaranteed.

Clark, Bueckers, Boston, Howard and Citron have all won multiple gold medals with USA Basketball at the youth level, from 2017 U16 gold in Argentina to finishing atop the podium at the 2019 U19 World Cup in Thailand, among others.

But as former USA Basketball national team director Carol Callan -- who oversaw all of the women's programs from 1996 to 2021 -- used to explain to players, those U17 and U19 World Cup teams would produce, on average, only one Olympian.

The World Cup is different from the Olympics, but "I think you could tell with those three specifically, they were all about basketball," Callan said of Clark, Bueckers and Boston. "Those three started at the top and they've maintained that. That's credit to them for not only their ability, but their drive, their mentality and the people that support them."

Howard has also been a mainstay for USA Basketball, featured on the Olympic qualifying team ahead of the Paris Games before ultimately being named to the 3x3 squad. Reese and Iriafen took less obvious paths: Iriafen first linked up with USA Basketball at December's training camp; Reese tried out for various youth national teams before making her first USA Basketball roster for the 2023 AmeriCup.

Callan said she ran into Reese at the event and "she just was so happy to be on a team, and I thought that was really great."

"You have two different ways to react to not making a team," Callan said. "One way is to just get angry and be done with it. And Angel persevered and made a team, and I can't say enough about her and how she's progressed to where she is today."

The sometimes-roundabout routes -- which for someone like Bueckers included missing significant time in college due to injury and falling out of the USA circuit -- makes being part of the senior national team now even sweeter.

"We all had different paths. We worked hard, had great faith. We just maintained our love and passion for the game," Bueckers said. "We're just grateful to be able to play at the national team level. Not everybody gets there. Not everybody has the same journey."

Added Clark: "I feel like there was just so much talent around my age group, and it's been fun to watch everybody kind of come into their own and have their own college careers and now live their dream at the professional level. ... It's just really cool, and feels like yesterday, honestly."

THE CHANGING OF the guard for USA Basketball started well before Berlin. The 2022 World Cup in Sydney was the USA's first major international competition since 2002 without Sue Bird or Diana Taurasi. Bird had announced her retirement, while Taurasi was injured.

Taurasi and Brittney Griner, who missed the 2022 World Cup while detained in Russia, were the most experienced members in Paris two years ago, though controversially neither saw much if any playing time in the final.

Breanna Stewart and Wilson had become the face of the USA Basketball dynasty, combining to win the past two MVPs at each of the Olympics and World Cup. The duo also accounted for 41% of the scoring at the Paris Games.

"We don't have that vet person; we are those people now," Stewart said recently.

Already a three-time Olympic gold medalist, Stewart, who recently turned 32, has a chance to join Bird as the only players to win four World Cup gold medals. She made her World Cup debut in 2014 at age 20.

"We are the ones who have been around the block a few times," Stewart told ESPN, "and it's exciting to help lead and guide them."

While a relatively inexperienced group, the United States is considered the favorite in Berlin, its roster loaded with young talent. Of the seven newcomers making their debut in a major international 5-on-5 competition, four were No. 1 picks in the WNBA draft and recent rookies of the year: Howard (2022), Boston (2023), Clark (2024) and Bueckers (2025).

Clark, Reese and Howard are leading the WNBA in assists (8.4), rebounds (12.4), and steals (2.4) per game, respectively. Clark and Bueckers are two of six players averaging at least 20 points. Citron and Iriafen are already multitime All-Stars despite being second-year players.

Clark, Bueckers, Reese, Howard and Iriafen already got a taste of what it's like to play for the senior national team, and Lawson, in March at the World Cup Qualifying tournament. In all, eight USA players who were in Puerto Rico -- including Chelsea Gray, Kahleah Copper and Jackie Young -- will also compete in Berlin. Clark and Bueckers were two of three players (alongside Plum) to play over 100 minutes in Puerto Rico and two of the top-four scorers for Team USA. Clark's 6.4 assists per game led the entire field, propelling her to earn MVP of the event.

Lawson has lauded Clark's play for the Indiana Fever this season, while the guard has said she hopes to be an extension of Lawson on the floor.

"They're both terrific," Lawson said while calling a WNBA game last month between Bueckers and Clark for Prime Video. "They're both about winning, which I think is the most important attribute in a player, in a great player."

While Clark and Bueckers might be the backcourt of the future, the ball is still expected to be primarily in the hands of Gray, the eldest player on the team at 33 and a two-time Olympic and 2022 World Cup gold medalist. But the younger guards will be watching closely to learn from her -- "I'll probably be annoying, I'll be asking so many questions," Bueckers said recently.

Stewart will anchor the effort in the frontcourt, but Reese, Boston and Iriafen will undoubtedly have even more responsibility now with Wilson out. Lawson has praised Reese for her impact on the glass -- her 8.0 boards in 16.7 minutes per game in Puerto Rico were second most in the tournament -- but has also said she sees the Dream star's physicality and competitive fire as translating well onto the FIBA stage.

"I just enjoy how she raises the level of a practice or of a game with her presence and with her intensity," Lawson said. "She plays with an aggression and a physicality, which I think is really important in FIBA play because there's a little more aggression and physicality that's typically allowed relative to the WNBA, and you need to have players that embrace that, and I think she's definitely one of the players on the roster that embraces that."

The combination of so much newness -- even Lawson was tabbed coach about a year ago -- and so little prep time is never ideal going into a major tournament, but that is typically how USA Basketball is forced to operate. The players and staff will lean on their time together in Puerto Rico or at training camps sprinkled across the past 10 months.

But they can also lean on the qualities that got them to Berlin. Lawson said her message to the younger players is to be themselves, and keep their mindset, confidence and belief in who they are intact no matter their role or experience.

"While they are kind of rookies, in my mind they're veterans," Callan said. "They infuse a competitiveness and an appreciation for the game that I think matches most those wily old veterans. You want some young ones that have this sort of really fun outlook on it, and I think they do [at the right times]. ... I think they'll bring a really nice mix to this team."

stories.headline: Atlanta Hawks offseason recap, early 2026-27 season preview
stories.summary: With the Trae Young era in the past, how do the Hawks move forward? We're looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season.
stories.body:
The Atlanta Hawks are entering the first full season of the post-Trae Young era with heightened expectations. After dealing their star point guard away last season, they've also moved on from 2024 No. 1 pick Zaccharie Risacher and brought in role players Aaron Wiggins, Ryan Nembhard and Luguentz Dort to strengthen their depth. CJ McCollum, the hero of their two first-round playoff wins against the eventual champion New York Knicks, is back as well, with Kingston Flemings, the No. 8 pick in the 2026 draft, backing him up.

ESPN's staff of experts is looking back at the offseason and taking an early look at the 2026-27 season for all 30 teams, with 30 pieces -- one for every team -- rolling out each weekday through Sept. 18. We're answering the biggest looming questions, evaluating X factors and much more for all 30 teams.

Quick links:

Roster | Depth chart | Transactions

More Hawks coverage | More NBA

Offseason at a glance
Key additions: Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Kingston Flemings, Devin Carter, Ryan Nembhard, Zuby Ejiofor, Henri Veesaar

Key retentions: CJ McCollum, Jock Landale

Key subtractions: Zaccharie Risacher, Jonathan Kuminga, Gabe Vincent, Keaton Wallace

Atlanta continued to move forward from the Trae Young trade last season by being opportunistic this offseason. The Hawks acquired Dort and Wiggins in separate trades from the Oklahoma City Thunder to add more help around emerging star Jalen Johnson. The Hawks also kept McCollum on a one-year, $21 million deal and drafted Flemings eighth overall. Atlanta is loaded with young wings looking to take a step forward under Quin Snyder like Nickeil Alexander-Walker did last season in winning Most Improved Player. -- Ohm Youngmisuk

Zach Kram's offseason grade: A-

Depending on how coach Quin Snyder structures his rotation, the Hawks might not have added a single starter this offseason -- although they did well to re-sign CJ McCollum to a solid one-year deal -- so their short-term ceiling still relies on Jalen Johnson's development into a star.

They made fairly dramatic upgrades to their bench, however, to meaningfully raise their floor. They acquired Luguentz Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Devin Carter in salary dump trades, as well as Ryan Nembhard to help stabilize the backcourt. -- Kram

What we learned over the past few months
From Ben Golliver's offseason lessons piece: Zaccharie Risacher was the biggest draft miss in years.

Evidently, Onsi Saleh, who was promoted to general manager last summer, had seen enough. The 46-win Hawks were better with Risacher off the court last season, and he seemingly lacks the burst, playmaking and takeover mentality to develop into a lead scoring option. While the 2024 draft was regarded as weak at the time, Risacher ranks 20th in his class by career win shares and has been outperformed by Stephon Castle and several other lottery picks, plus a few players drafted 20-plus spots after him, including Baylor Scheierman, Kyle Filipowski and Oso Ighodaro.

Risacher's value dropped to the point that the Hawks didn't recoup a first-round pick in their three-team trade with the Mavericks and Oklahoma City Thunder. Instead, they added guards Luguentz Dort and Ryan Nembhard as they continue to build out their depth in the post-Trae Young era. -- Golliver

The big question: Can Johnson take the next step and win a playoff series?
Johnson averaged 22.5 points, 10.3 rebounds and 7.9 assists last season when Atlanta pivoted from Young and handed over the keys to the franchise to the versatile 6-8 forward. Johnson made the All-Star team and helped Atlanta become the only team to take two games off the eventual champion Knicks. But they also blew a 2-1 lead by losing three straight, including suffering an embarrassing 140-89 loss in Game 6 to New York. That should have left a lasting bitter taste for the Hawks all offseason and motivate Johnson to show he can take another step forward and lead the Hawks to a playoff series victory as their main star. -- Youngmisuk

Basketball Power Index rank: No. 17

The Hawks' starting unit last year was the second-best unit in the league (at least 400 possessions together). The Hornets' was best and they broke it up; Atlanta is sticking with it (unless rumors of Dort starting are true). The Hawks were 19-21 and ninth in the East before acquiring a key part of that lineup in CJ McCollum. They were 27-15 the rest of the way and beat the Knicks twice in the playoffs. -- Dean Oliver

Post-free agency Power Rankings: Hawks are No. 14

Biggest X factor
C Onyeka Okongwu

The Hawks are bursting with perimeter depth after trading for Dort and Wiggins, drafting Flemings and re-signing McCollum to a one-year deal. But Jock Landale -- a fine backup but not remotely a quality NBA starter -- provides the only depth at center, which means the starter, Okongwu, has a great deal of responsibility resting on his shoulders.

Okongwu developed into a capable stretch big last season, making 38% of his 5.2 3-point attempts per game. But he still needs to gain more scoring efficiency overall, as well as serve as a strong backline defender behind Dort, Dyson Daniels and the rest of Atlanta's perimeter stoppers. -- Kram

The Hawks traded Trae Young on Jan. 7, and after that trade finished with a 29-15 regular-season record that was the seventhbest in the NBA in that span. The Hawks then went up 2-1 on the eventual champion Knicks in the playoffs, the only team to win two games against New York during the playoffs. The Hawks return their core that finished the season, led by budding star Jalen Johnson, and supplemented that with two contributors from the Oklahoma City Thunder championship team (Dort and Wiggins) as well as a lottery pick in Flemings. They seem poised to continue and improve upon their strong finish in the upcoming campaign. -- Andre' Snellings

stories.headline: Fenerbahce: Mason Greenwood, Matteo Guendouzi subject of UEFA investigation
stories.summary: Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.
stories.body:
Mason Greenwood and Matteo Guendouzi are the subject of a disciplinary investigation by UEFA, Fenerbahce have confirmed.

Fenerbahce's 2-1 win away at Lyon in a Champions League qualifier ended amid ugly scenes involving Greenwood and Guendouzi who both previously played for Marseille, the rivals of Lyon.

Guendouzi raised his middle finger to Lyon fans during the warmup and after the game and shouted "Allez l'OM" ("Go Marseille"), also grabbing his crotch, in wild post-match scenes. He said Lyon fans insulted his family before and during the game.

A post-match scuffle included someone wearing Lyon club colours confronting Guendouzi, before several players became involved in an incident in the tunnel.

It was unclear if UEFA's disciplinary judges will sanction the players before Fenerbahce opens the Champions League main phase next Thursday, hosting Roma. Fenerbahce's second game is at Aston Villa on Oct. 14.

A Fenerbahce statement read: "Following the UEFA Champions League playoff round second leg match, UEFA has initiated disciplinary proceedings against our players Matteo Guendouzi and Mason Greenwood, as well as against our club.

"Our club will present the necessary defences before the relevant UEFA bodies in order to protect the rights and interests of our players and Fenerbahce during this process.

"The necessary information, documents and defences regarding the process will be submitted to UEFA, and developments are being closely monitored by our club. We hereby inform the public."

Fenerbahce qualified for the Champions League for the first time since 2008-09 at Lyon's expense after a 3-2 aggregate win.

Former Manchester United striker Greenwood joined the Turkish club this summer from Marseille in a €39 million ($44.5m) deal.

stories.headline: Winners and losers of Cale Makar's $163.2 million contract
stories.summary: The deal for Colorado's franchise defenseman set a new high benchmark for NHL players, with impacts around the league.
stories.body:
Cale Makar made NHL history last week, becoming the first player to earn $20 million annually in his blockbuster contract extension with the Colorado Avalanche.

His deal is worth $163.2 million over 8 seasons. The 27-year-old defenseman's average annual value is $20.8 million against the salary cap. While many anticipated Makar would set new standards with his new contract, the fallout from his deal with Colorado will impact the rest of the NHL.

Some teams, players and trends will end up winners because of it. Others ... not so much.

Here are some winners and losers of the Cale Makar contract.

Winner: Colorado Avalanche
Obviously.

GM Joe Sakic said recently that "you can't win without superstars." That's what you'd expect to hear from a guy who won Stanley Cups as a player on teams that featured Hall of Famers like Peter Forsberg, Ray Bourque, Rob Blake and this guy Patrick Roy in goal; but also from the guy who built a roster around Makar and center Nathan MacKinnon that produced a Stanley Cup win back in 2022.

There's an argument to be made that the Avalanche have the best players in the world at center and on defense and now have them both locked up through 2031. Every team in the league is trying to build a winner. No one has that kind of foundation on which to build.

Sakic was blessed with a star defenseman who wanted to go max term (eight years) from the start of negotiations. No "wait and see" contract. No trying to sync up the end of his deal with that of a family member on another NHL team (more on that in a moment). Cale Makar wanted to give Colorado nine whacks at the pinata while he's under contract.

We can tsk tsk the Avalanche for not leveraging that commitment into a friendlier cap hit, but the reality is that both Makar and his camp fully understood the current market and the one that Makar could create as an unrestricted free agent next summer. There was no steep discount to be had here, nor should there have been the expectation of one.

There are legit concerns about aging curves and overall health for a player that logs the kind of ice time that Makar does. Teams go into contract talks all the time with that in the back of their throats. But the inherent greatness of Makar, and this window to win with him on the blue line, outweigh those worries.

His cap hit will be recontextualized, as they all eventually are. The NHL is going to have the revenue streams from new media rights deals and at least two new teams inflating the cap during Makar's contract term. As one player agent told me: "By the time this deal is over, there will be guys in the league making $30 million per season."

Loser: Bill Guerin
First off, much respect to the Minnesota GM for facing a barrage of questions during a recent local media tour -- at the Minnesota State Fair, no less! -- about the status of his contract negotiations with Quinn Hughes. We've come to expect that kind of candor from Guerin, as both an NHL executive and U.S. national team general manager, but it's still refreshing when so many of his colleagues get camera shy during high-stakes negotiations.

Guerin told WCCO's Chad Hartman that there's "no tension" with Hughes and his agent Pat Brisson, but refused to traffic in hypotheticals. Dan Barreiro of KFAN told Guerin he "can't trade" Hughes due to how much the Wild gave the Vancouver Canucks for the defenseman; Guerin reiterated that "we don't want to lose him and our fans don't want to lose him."

Hughes has one more season left at $7.85 million before becoming an unrestricted free agent next summer, and he's eligible to sign an extension now. If he signs before Sept. 15, he can max out at an eight-year term. If he signs as a free agent next summer, the max is six years -- although the max contract he could sign (20% of a projected $113.5 million cap in 2027-28) would be higher, at $22.7 million.

It's hard to find many around the NHL that believe Hughes will sign a long-term deal with the Wild. Most expect it'll be a three-year term that walks him up to 2030 when his brother Jack Hughes of the New Jersey Devils is an unrestricted free agent. But what about the money?

As Guerin did radio hits about Hughes amid the butter sculptures and lumberjack shows at the fair, there was one common theme: That Makar's deal impacts what Hughes could make on a new contract, but not dramatically.

"Could it affect you financially? Yeah. There's the bar with Cale Makar signing that contract in Colorado, but Quinn might be after different things. He's got different things in the life that's important to him," he told Hartman.

Guerin's theory: That Hughes has already made significant money in his career, so he can afford to make different types of decisions on his next contract. His current contract, signed in 2021, is worth $47.1 million.

"It doesn't have to be that 'Makar signed for this so he's gotta sign for that.' No. He can do whatever the hell he wants because he's not going broke tomorrow," Guerin told KFAN.

Of course, Makar will have made $54 million on his current deal before starting on a $163 million contract in 2027-28.

It's possible that Guerin would have to overcompensate Hughes regardless of what Makar makes, like he did to keep Kirill Kaprizov in Minnesota. Makar's deal doesn't dramatically change the math on Hughes. It also doesn't uncomplicate what's already an extremely complicated negotiation for Guerin.

Winner: Matthew Schaefer
After just one season with the New York Islanders -- in which he was the unanimous choice for NHL rookie of the year -- Schaefer might already be in blank check territory for his next contract. The defenseman, who turns 19 this week, has that rare franchise-altering alchemy of on-ice ability and off-ice charisma that's been previously exhibited by players like Alex Ovechkin. He's that special.

And soon he'll be very, very rich.

Schaefer can sign an extension next summer as he enters the last year of his rookie contract. Islanders GM Mathieu Darche now has two contractual magnets pulling up Schaefer's salary: Makar, resetting the bar for defensemen at $20.4 million AAV; and San Jose Sharks phenom Macklin Celebrini, another transformative young player who will earn $18.8 annually over five seasons.

Loser: Columbus Blue Jackets
The current holy trinity of NHL defensemen is Makar, Hughes and Zach Werenski, the latter of whom won the Norris Trophy last season ... and then blocked a trade to the Dallas Stars after communicating that he didn't plan on signing an extension with the Blue Jackets.

Werenski, 29, has since emphasized that he wants to remain in Columbus as long as the Blue Jackets are a playoff team that's trending in the right direction.

He's eligible to sign an extension next summer, with two years remaining on a deal that carries a $9,583,334 average annual value. The ceiling for Werenski as a 2028 free agent would be an AAV of $24.6 million. Whether or not his heart's still in Columbus could be a separate issue from whether or not the Blue Jackets would commit that kind of money for any player -- let alone a defenseman that'll be in his early 30s by then.

Winner: Montreal Canadiens
Lane Hutson finished one point behind Cale Makar in scoring among defensemen last season. In 2027-28, when he's 23 years old, Hutson will count $11.55 million less against the salary cap than Makar does.

There are mitigating circumstances for Montreal's deal with Hutson, which he signed last October in the final season of his rookie contract. The defenseman was a 10.2(c) restricted free agent, leaving him with little leverage as a player ineligible for either an offer sheet or arbitration. But Montreal used that advantage to squeeze an eight-year deal with an $8.85 million annual cap hit out of Hutson.

It was praised as a bargain at the time -- many felt he'd at least hit $10 million AAV -- but given how the ground shifted after Makar's deal for scoring defensemen, it's an absolute steal.

This is going to be for Montreal like MacKinnon's second contract was for Colorado (seven years at $6.3 million annually): an epic underpayment of an elite player that allows his team to get a ton of other business done. Keep in mind the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in Year 6 of that deal.

Loser: Analytics truthers
Cale Makar has been a Norris Trophy finalist in six of his seven NHL seasons, winning it twice and finishing second in the voting twice as well. He's got a Calder Trophy and a Conn Smythe to his credit. He's considered the best defenseman of his generation, perhaps even the best player of his generation. Comparisons to Bobby Orr aren't met with a scoff but with respectful contemplation.

But there's another assessment of Makar -- in the present and for the duration of his contract -- that's worth considering: The one from analytics-driven skeptics who see Makar's deified status as more than a little bit owed to the greatness of MacKinnon.

Corey Sznajder had a nuanced look at this theory on All Three Zones, which included these numbers from Natural Stat Trick:

"Over the past three seasons, Makar has shared the ice with MacKinnon for 2,572 minutes compared to 1,434 minutes without him (all 5v5 by the way). In those minutes, the Avs own 58.1% of the shot attempts, 57.4% of the Expected Goals and 61.3% of the goals. In the minutes with Makar without MacKinnon the ice, Colorado owns only 47.3% of the shots, 48% of the Expected Goals and 52.2% of the goals. MacKinnon without Makar on the ice is at 56.6%, 55.7% and 66.8% in all three of those stats respectively," Sznajder wrote.

Those kinds of stats don't necessarily paint their on-ice partnership as symbiotic, but rather MacKinnon being the one driving the bus, while Makar stands over his shoulder like Keanu with Sandra Bullock in "Speed."

Obviously, the Avalanche don't care about any of this after giving Makar a record-breaking contract. He and MacKinnon are going to share the ice for Colorado until 2031 at a minimum. But this conjecture will continue to simmer in awards debates, player comparisons on social media and now in evaluating Makar under this mega-deal.

Winner: Player Empowerment
As I wrote back in June, the age of player empowerment is at hand for the NHL. We saw it in Brady Tkachuk leveraging a trade to his brother's team in South Florida, or in Dylan Larkin trying to force his way out of a long-term commitment to the Detroit Red Wings. But we also saw it in some of the mega-contracts that we signed in the offseason, with Makar's deal as the current apex.

Young stars like Celebrini ($18.8 million AAV) and Chicago's Connor Bedard ($15 million AAV) scored big in re-signing with their teams. Leo Carlsson shocked the NHL by signing a five-year, $18 million AAV offer sheet with the Philadelphia Flyers that the Anaheim Ducks matched.

(My favorite theory of the offseason, offered up by one NHL player agent: That Flyers ownership greenlit the Carlsson offer sheet as the ultimate long-term vengeance in the Cutter Gauthier drama with Anaheim. "They probably want to say, 'Hey, Philly's a good spot to be in. Don't [mess] with us.'")

There are always going to be players that take a "team-friendly" deal because the circumstances warrant it, like Connor McDavid earning less annually than Leon Draisaitl. But the ones breaking the bank are no longer the outliers, and they're going to keep breaking it. Some NHL teams are projecting the salary cap could rise to $150-$160 million by the 2031-32 season. Makar is just the beginning.

(Although, technically, Makar did just sign a team-friendly deal: $400,000 annually under the max, and one year before unrestricted free agency could have upped his ask to over $22 million annually.)

Loser: Short-term deals
Perhaps the most shocking aspect of Makar's extension wasn't the money but the term.

One hallmark of the NHL's player empowerment trend has been contract duration. Auston Matthews was one of the first huge names to go short-term, signing a five-year deal with the Toronto Maple Leafs in 2019 and then a four-year extension in 2023. Since then, Celebrini, Bedard, Carlsson and Nico Hischier of the New Jersey Devils have all signed five-year extensions, while defenseman Evan Bouchard went four years with the Edmonton Oilers.

But Makar's focus from the start of talks with the Avalanche was an eight-year term, an option that will not exist when the new CBA kicks in later this month.

"I think it gives us a lot of clarity in the sense of the direction we want to go in, hopefully being able to succeed in the next nine years, and have that stability in knowing that the contract is there and we have the pieces that we can build around," he said, via NHL.com.

Again, not everyone in the NHL can look around their locker room and see Nathan MacKinnon, with the proof of concept of having already won a Stanley Cup with him. Makar didn't have to take the "wait and see" deal that others in his tax bracket have with teams striving to become contenders. Makar knows what he has around him. And now, the Avalanche know they have Makar for the next decade.

McLaren's Lando Norris sealed back-to-back victories after winning the Dutch Grand Prix to kick off the second half of the season last time out.

The "Temple of Speed" is known for its long straights and heavy braking zones, and is the fastest track in Formula 1 history by overall average lap speed.

It's another classic circuit that has been on the calendar since 1950, only missing one year of racing in 1980 due to upgrading the track infrastructure.

It has one of the best podiums in the world as the famous Ferrari-loving tifosi flood onto the track after the race is finished. It's always a sight to be seen, especially if you are a Ferrari driver or an Italian driver.

Italian Grand Prix

Circuit: Autodromo Nazionale Monza; Monza, Italy

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg, Mercedes

2017: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2018: Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes

2019: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2020: Pierre Gasly, AlphaTauri

2021: Daniel Ricciardo, McLaren

2022: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2023: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

2024: Charles Leclerc, Ferrari

2025: Max Verstappen, Red Bull

Other key stats

First F1 race: 1950

Lap record: 1:18.792, Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Laps: 53 laps of 5.8km. Total distance 306km

Most poles: Lewis Hamilton has seven at this circuit (2009, 2012, 2014-2017, 2020). Other pole sitters from the grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022), Max Verstappen (2021 and 2025), Carlos Sainz (2023) and Lando Norris (2024).

Most wins: Lewis Hamilton (2012, 2014-2015, 2017-2018) and Michael Schumacher (1996, 1998, 2000, 2003, 2006) are tied on five wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Fernando Alonso (2007, 2010), Pierre Gasly (2020), Charles Leclerc (2019, 2024) and Max Verstappen (2022, 2023 and 2025).

Weather forecast

The weather for the Italian Grand Prix is forecast to be sunny all weekend with light winds, with highs of 32°C on Sunday.

What happened last year?

Max Verstappen set the pace with the fastest lap in F1 history after getting pole position in Monza.

The Dutchman set a time of 1:18.792 breaking Hamilton's record from 2020.

It was McLaren's Norris who was on provisional pole before Verstappen beat him to the line in the closing stages.

Verstappen then went on to win the race in commanding fashion, but there were some team orders taking place at McLaren.

Norris was running in second for the majority of the race, but after a slow pit-stop, the team asked Oscar Piastri to move aside and let him teammate back through for second place.

At the time, Piastri was leading the championship from Norris by 31 points.

Who will win this year?

The biggest news entering the weekend will be Antonelli's engine penalty that will hamper his opportunity to score maximum points during the race.

He leads the championship after winning six races, but title fights can change quickly, as we saw during the backend of the 2025 season.

McLaren's upgrades have certainly been working, but team boss Andrea Stella said that Monza will be the true benchmark in terms of its performance and progress.

Ferrari will be hungry to get a home win with either of its drivers, but Monza will typically suit those strong in straight line speed and high-speed corners, such as Mercedes.

Monza could be one of the best opportunities to close the gap in the title race and take advantage of Antonelli not being a threat at the front of the pack.

stories.headline: State of Origin: Darius Boyd replaces Billy Slater as Queensland coach
stories.summary: Queensland's search for a new State of Origin coach is over, with Maroons legend Darius Boyd to take over in 2027 after signing a two-year deal.
stories.body:
Former Queensland star Darius Boyd will lean on the legacy and advice of former mentors Mal Meninga and Wayne Bennett after being appointed as the new Maroons coach.

The Queensland Rugby League confirmed on Thursday that Boyd would take up the position in 2027 on a two-year deal after Billy Slater stepped down from the role after five years.

Boyd, who won NRL premierships with Brisbane and St George Illawarra in a 337-game career, played 28 State of Origin matches for the Maroons and was a key figure in the dynasty under Meninga.

As a coach Boyd has led the Queensland U19 team to wins in back-to-back interstate clashes after being a member of the coaching staff at the Broncos under Kevin Walters for three seasons.

Boyd, who also played 23 Tests for Australia, said he was "extremely honoured" to be entrusted with coaching Queensland's State of Origin team.

"It's a privileged position and I'm very grateful for the opportunity," Boyd said.

"I understand the responsibility that comes with the role as well. My job is to build on the legacy created by the many great Queensland players and coaches who have come before us."

Boyd, who said Slater had left behind a wonderful program to build on, will make a call on his staff in the future, but said those who "live and breathe" for the jersey will be at the top of his list.

He played most of his career under his lifelong mentor Wayne Bennett, who has said he would assist the new coach where he can.

"He is the supercoach. I would be silly not to get his advice on things," Boyd said when asked if Bennett would be on his team.

Meninga, who coached Boyd in the glory years, also shaped the way he will approach the task.

Boyd said that "the history and what it meant to play for Queensland and how Origin started and the legacy those guys left behind" was a key message of Meninga that got the best out of the Maroons.

"It is a challenging job to be out in the cauldron and play at the highest level and perform at your best," Boyd said.

"Mal was really good at getting the best out of you emotionally and mentally and making sure you were prepared come game night."

QRL chairman Brian Canavan said once Slater stepped down after winning three of five series, the organisation came up with a list of candidates and Boyd was the standout.

"If you go back five years ago Billy was at the same point," he said.

"He hadn't had the formal NRL coaching experience. Darius has more experience than Billy had back then. That gave us confidence to go to a new phase.

"Billy has left the place and program in great shape, and Darius will step in and put his own spin on things.":

Bennett was a great support on and off the field to Boyd and will be there to lean on.

"The advice Wayne offered was that he would support whoever we appointed, and Wayne has had a long association with Darius and knows his great strengths," Canavan said.

"The most important thing for this job is the identity with the state.

"What he has got is the pride and passion for the jersey and the state and this connection with players and appetite for the historical aspects of the jersey and embedding it in players."

Boyd entered a mental health facility at a key moment in his NRL career and has since been a leader in that space.

It was a turning point and he now understands the mental side of life and footy.

"It has been a journey for me on and off the field. It is a great opportunity for me to instil belief, confidence and desire into the next generation," he said.

stories.headline: Mike Dean admits to playing secret 'game' to not blow whistle while refereeing Premier League matches
stories.summary: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean has revealed he used to play secret "games" while refereeing top-flight matches, including one where he tried to avoid giving a foul for as long as possible.
stories.body:
Former Premier League referee Mike Dean has revealed he used to play secret "games" while refereeing top-flight matches, including one where he tried to avoid giving a foul for as long as possible.

Speaking on the Jamie Vardy's Having a Party podcast, Dean admitted to playing two different "games," and suggested he had also discussed playing them with other officials.

"There used to be games we used to have, as a laugh we used to say 'Right, we'll kick off now, right. See how long we can go without blowing a whistle,'" he said.

"I've done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20-25 minutes without blowing a whistle -- 'Let it go, let it go, let it go.'"

Dean also revealed he played a second game where he would challenge himself to stay inside the centre circle for as long as possible.

"I used to do another thing in the Premier League," he said. "I used to stand in the centre circle and see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about.

"The lads used to be on the line saying 'You can't.' I said 'I'll try it.'

"You'd just, like, kind of run round, kind of go ... But don't come out of it [the centre circle]. I got about 15 minutes once, in one game, without leaving the centre circle."

Dean did not give any examples of specific matches when he played these "games." VAR was introduced in 2019 which means that, if he did play the "games" before its introduction, it would have been under Pro Ref's previous leadership.

Pro Ref declined to comment when contacted by ESPN. ESPN also reached out to the Premier League for comment.

In 2023, following a game a year before between Chelsea and Tottenham in which he was the VAR, Dean admitted to not alerting referee Anthony Taylor to a missed call because he wanted to spare him "more grief."

Dean, who served solely as a VAR during the 2022-23 season having retired from refereeing in 2022, stepped back from officiating altogether in 2023.
